place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 柴房 · 开春

setup.zh: 除夕，周衡落下一本旧账，一行字后头没有数：十月十八。漳水。阿姊。正月初一，他给了你一块执事堂的牌子：差事，自己挣。正月里，家里的回信到了。开了春，月底你去执事堂交差，周衡把一篮残株推了过来——巡夜的工钱。
setup.en: New Year's Eve: Zhou Heng drops an old ledger, and one line in it has no figure after it: The eighteenth of the tenth month. The Zhang. Sister. On New Year's Day he gives you a Stewards' Hall tag: errands — earn your own way. In the first month the letter from home comes. In spring, when you go to the Stewards' Hall at the month's end to hand in your errand, Zhou Heng pushes a basket of culls across to you — the night watch's pay.

recap.zh: 除夕，周衡的旧账上一行没有数的字：十月十八。漳水。阿姊。正月初一，执事堂两面墙：东墙杂役，西墙差事，打妖的红牌五层以下不许揭。开春的残株——巡夜的工钱——一株一株喂进饭桶，开出三颗聚气丹——一纹、二纹、九纹各一；分堆一认，认出三张方子——方子管出什么丹，纹是运气；缸是饭桶涨的，层是崖顶上定风过的，三月里过了五层；灵石先见了底。阿禾、孙二狗的书案底下，各多了一个油纸包：二狗的二纹，阿禾的那一颗九纹。
recap.en: New Year's Eve: a line with no figure in Zhou Heng's old ledger: The eighteenth of the tenth month. The Zhang. Sister. New Year's Day: the two walls of the Stewards' Hall — servants' work on the east, errands on the west; the red monster-hunting tags not to be taken below the fifth layer. The spring culls — the night watch's pay — went into the Rice Bucket one by one and gave three Qi-Gathering Pills — one of one line, one of two, one of nine; sorted into heaps, they gave up three recipes — the recipe decides which pill, the lines are luck; the Rice Bucket filled the vat, and the layer was crossed on the clifftop by stilling the wind: past the fifth in the third month; the spirit stones ran out first. Under Ahe's desk and Sun Ergou's, an oilpaper packet each: Ergou's the two-line, Ahe's the nine.

en: The letter from home in the first month: the roof is mended.
A basket of culls, the night watch's pay.
Three: one line, two lines, nine lines.

story.zh:
除夕那夜，观里空了一半，那一夜，他十四了。周衡在执事房里点了一整根蜡烛，把留山的几个弟子都叫了去，每人分了一碗饺子。周衡坐在桌子后头，看着他们吃，自己一个也没动。

小满洗完七只碗，这才瞧见桌角上还落着一本账。翻开的那一页纸已黄透了，字写得歪歪扭扭，一看便是小孩子的手笔。这一页的末了，只有一行字，却写得极用力：

**十月十八。漳水。阿姊。**

他刚走到廊下，便听见了周衡的声音：「……观主，今年，让弟子去吧。」观主的声音很和气：「十天的路。那条河里的事，不是练气的人管得了的。」又道：「邺城那桩事，说是给河伯娶媳妇，其实是有人借河伯的名头，年年从百姓手里敛钱。要去，也得是个筑了基的，不然有去无回——外门里，今年没人筑基。」周衡道：「……是。明年，弟子再来。」

小满把那本旧账簿递过去：「你落下的。」周衡接过来，看了看他，道：「看了？」小满道：「……看周师兄的字好。」十月十八，漳水，筑了基的——这三样，他记下了。

后来，他从邓执事嘴里听说了周衡的事。他八岁那年，阿姊十五，叫河伯庙的巫祝挑中了。十月十八那天，他追着那只船，在漳水边上跑了二里地，船到了河当中，一斜，就没了。「他算了一辈子的账，就这一笔，他平不了。」

正月初一领灵石，小满把腰上那块巡夜令解下来，放在桌上。周衡看也没看，拿指头推了回来：「空着也是空着。」顿了一顿，又道：「挂着它，园里少一株，戒律堂头一个问你。」

周衡又从抽屉里摸出一块牌子，拍在桌上，刻着三个字：执事堂。「差事牌挂在执事堂，揭一块，办一桩。」他顿了一顿，「打妖的红牌，五层以下，不许揭。」

西墙是内门的，牌子分颜色。红木的是除妖：「蒙山北灵草谷，夜里有妖，六层，未开灵智，吃灵草，伤人。每人二十块灵石。」有的名字底下，画着一道黑线。墙的最高一排，单钉着一块黑牌，没有字，只刻着一个地名：「泗水 · 渡口」。

守执事堂的是个独臂的执事，姓邓：「看懂了？」小满道：「黑线是……」邓执事道：「牌子揭了，人没回来。」他把草鞋翻了个面，「内门三十年，十一道。」小满又问：「最上头那一块——」邓执事道：「那是黑牌。牌上不写什么事，事我当面跟你说。」他抬起头，看了小满一眼，「九层以后再来看。」

正月里，家里的回信到了。他娘的字小，写得密：屋顶修了；五两银子腊月里送到了，你爹便再没往黑松岭那头去过。末了一句是：吴婆婆让我捎一句话给你，她说：「告诉那孩子，牙还在。」我问她什么牙，她不说，只是笑。
story.en:
On New Year's Eve the abbey was half empty. That night he turned fourteen. In the stewards' office Zhou Heng lit a whole candle, called in the few disciples who'd stayed on the mountain, and gave each of them a bowl of dumplings. Zhou Heng sat behind the table and watched them eat, and didn't touch one himself.

Xiaoman washed the seven bowls, and only then noticed a ledger left on the corner of the table. The page it was open at had gone completely yellow. The writing was crooked and wobbly; one look told you it was a child's hand. At the end of the page there was only one line, but it was written so hard the strokes had gone through the paper:

**Eighteenth of the tenth month. The Zhang River. Sister.**

He had just reached the gallery when he heard Zhou Heng's voice: "...Abbot, this year, let me go." The Abbot's voice was gentle. "It's ten days' road. What's in that river isn't something a Qi Condensation cultivator can deal with." After a while he went on: "That business in Ye: they call it finding a bride for the River Lord, but really someone is using the River Lord's name to squeeze money out of the common people every year. But whoever goes has to have Foundation Establishment, or he won't come back. In the outer sect, no one reached Foundation Establishment this year." Zhou Heng said, "...Yes. Next year, I'll come again."

Xiaoman held out the old ledger: "You left this." Zhou Heng took it, looked at him and said, "Did you read it?" Xiaoman said, "...Senior brother Zhou has good handwriting." The eighteenth of the tenth month, the Zhang River, someone with Foundation Establishment: those three things he kept.

Later he heard about Zhou Heng from Steward Deng. The year he was eight and his sister fifteen, the shamans of the River Lord's temple picked her. On the eighteenth of the tenth month, he chased that boat along the bank of the Zhang River for two li; the boat reached the middle of the river, tipped, and was gone. "He's kept accounts all his life, and that's the one entry he can't balance."

On the first day of the first month, spirit stones were handed out. Xiaoman untied the night-watch token from his waist and set it on the table. Zhou Heng didn't even look at it, and pushed it back with one finger: "It'll only sit empty." After a pause he added, "Keep wearing it. If the garden's one plant short, the Discipline Hall asks you first."

Zhou Heng took another tablet out of the drawer and slapped it on the table, carved with three characters: Stewards' Hall. "The errand tablets hang in the Stewards' Hall. Take one, do one job." He paused. "The red tablets, for fighting demons: below the fifth layer, you may not take them."

The west wall belonged to the inner sect, and the tablets came in colours. The red wood ones were demon-killing: "Spirit Herb Valley, north of Mount Meng: a demon at night, sixth layer, no spirit wisdom yet, eats spirit herbs, hurts people. Twenty spirit stones each." Under some of the names a black line was drawn. On the topmost row of the wall hung a single black tablet, with no writing, only a place name carved on it: "The Si River · The Ferry".

The steward who kept the Stewards' Hall had one arm and was named Deng: "Understand it?" Xiaoman said, "The black lines are..." Steward Deng said, "The tablet was taken and the man didn't come back." He turned the sandal over. "Thirty years of the inner sect: eleven lines." Xiaoman asked again, "The one at the very top—" Steward Deng said, "That's a black tablet. It doesn't say what the job is. The job, I tell you face to face." He looked up and gave Xiaoman a look. "Come and look again after the ninth layer."

In the first month, the answer from home arrived. Mother's writing was small and close: the roof was mended; the five taels of silver had arrived in the twelfth month, and your Pa hasn't gone up towards Black Pine Ridge since. The last line said: Granny Wu asked me to pass something on to you. She said, "Tell the boy the tooth's still there." I asked her what tooth, and she wouldn't say, only laughed.

story_full.zh:
除夕那夜，观里空了一半，家近的都告了假回家过年，那一夜，他十四了。

周衡那夜破了例。他在执事房里点了一整根蜡烛——不是半根，是一整根——把留山的几个弟子都叫了去，每人分了一碗饺子。饺子是白菜馅的，一碗十二个，不多不少。周衡坐在桌子后头，看着他们吃，自己一个也没动。

众人吃完了饺子，一个一个道了谢散了。周衡却站起身来，把账簿往胳膊底下一夹，道：「沈小满，碗洗了。」说罢，出门往正殿那边去了。

小满洗完七只碗，这才瞧见桌角上还落着一本账。极旧，比周衡平日背着的那本小了一圈，书皮磨得发亮。周衡这人，一根蜡烛掰几截都要记，从没落下过一样东西；今夜偏偏把它落下了，还翻开着。

翻开的那一页纸已黄透了，上面记的全是些零零碎碎的小账：「豆子二升，十四文」「盐半斤」「阿姊的头绳，三文」，字写得歪歪扭扭，一看便是小孩子的手笔。这一页的末了，只有一行字，却写得极用力，笔画都戳破了纸：

**十月十八。漳水。阿姊。**

小满瞧了好一会儿，才想明白哪里不对：周衡的账，每一行后头都跟着一个数，一株草，三块灵石，半根蜡烛。只有这一行，后头什么也没有。

他合上账簿，揣进怀里，去正殿还他。正殿的门虚掩着，里头点着一盏灯。他刚走到廊下，便听见了周衡的声音。那声音他从没听过，不像记账，倒像求人：「……观主，今年，让弟子去吧。」

观主的声音很和气：「十天的路。那条河里的事，不是练气的人管得了的。你去了，周家便又少一个。」隔了一会儿，又道：「邺城那桩事，说是给河伯娶媳妇，其实是有人借河伯的名头，年年从百姓手里敛钱，敛钱的人背后，站着一个大宗门。观里的长老去了，便是沉鼎观跟人家翻脸；一个外门出身的弟子揭一块牌子去了，才只是一桩差事。要去，也得是个筑了基的，不然有去无回——外门里，今年没人筑基。」

殿里静了很久。周衡道：「……是。明年，弟子再来。」

小满往廊柱后头一缩。周衡从殿里出来，走得很慢。小满把那本旧账簿递过去：「你落下的。」周衡接过来，看了看他，道：「看了？」小满道：「……看周师兄的字好。」周衡把账簿揣进怀里，走了。

小满在廊下站了一会儿。十月十八，漳水，筑了基的——这三样，他记下了。

后来，他从邓执事嘴里听说了周衡的事。周衡是邺城人，爹死得早，家里就他跟一个阿姊。他八岁那年，阿姊十五，叫河伯庙的巫祝挑中了，说是河伯看上的媳妇。十月十八那天，他追着那只船，在漳水边上跑了二里地，船到了河当中，一斜，就没了。第二年他背着一捆柴上了蒙山，进了沉鼎观，一待快二十年。「他图的不是报仇。」邓执事道，「那条河里，年年还要沉一个。他算了一辈子的账，就这一笔，他平不了。」

正月初一领灵石，周衡坐在饭堂门口那张桌子后头发。小满入了内门的名册，外门的差事照理要交回去，他便把腰上那块巡夜令解下来，放在桌上。周衡看也没看，拿指头推了回来：「空着也是空着。」顿了一顿，又道：「挂着它，园里少一株，戒律堂头一个问你。」

周衡又从抽屉里摸出一块牌子，拍在桌上。这一块不是乌木的，是松木，巴掌长，刻着三个字：执事堂。「内门的人，账上多一样：差事。差事牌挂在执事堂，揭一块，办一桩；办成了，牌子翻过来，照牌上的数领工钱。杂役，外门也揭得；采办、护送，内门的人揭。」他顿了一顿，「打妖的红牌，五层以下，不许揭。」

执事堂在正殿西边，一间空屋，没有神像，只有两面墙。

东墙上的牌子是乌木的，一色的黑，巴掌长，字是白粉填的：「伙房 · 帮厨」「山道 · 挑水」「藏经阁 · 抄经」「丹房 · 看丹炉」「兽栏 · 喂灵兽」「符房 · 补符纸」。这些牌子不打架，是外门的杂役，谁揭都成；揭了去执事房找周衡领差，工钱不是灵石，是「功」——周衡账上记一笔；也有拿东西付的，帮厨的一个月领一坛腌菜。东墙上有一枚钉子是空的，钉子底下的白粉字还在：「药园 · 巡夜」。小满在那枚空钉子跟前站了一站。去年秋天周衡在执事房里说「药园巡夜，沈小满。工钱，残株，月一篮」，他只当是周衡随口派的一桩苦差；原来那块牌子，是从这面墙上摘下来的，在他腰里挂了一个冬天了。

西墙是内门的，牌子分颜色。白木的是采办：「赤芝三朵，坊市钱掌柜收。灵石一块。」黄木的是护送：「下邳药商一车，走北道。灵石三块。」红木的是除妖：「蒙山北灵草谷，夜里有妖，六层，未开灵智，吃灵草，伤人。每人二十块灵石。」「下邳北道，山路吃人，三条命。灵石三块。」青木的是寻人：「沛县西乡，走失男孩一名，七岁，左耳一颗痣。银五钱。」乌木的也有几块，写的是观里的事：「藏经阁晒书，三日。记功。」一块挨一块，像一面墙的牙。也有翻过来的，背面一个朱红的「讫」字，底下钉一块小的，写几个人名。有的名字底下，画着一道黑线。

墙的最高一排，单钉着一块黑牌，没有字，只刻着一个地名：「泗水 · 渡口」。小满看了半天，没看懂。

守执事堂的是个独臂的执事，姓邓，坐在门槛上编草鞋，头也不抬：「看懂了？」小满道：「黑线是……」邓执事道：「牌子揭了，人没回来。」他把草鞋翻了个面，「内门三十年，十一道。」小满又问：「最上头那一块——」邓执事道：「那是黑牌。一年也就挂出一块，顶多两块。牌上不写什么事，事我当面跟你说。」他抬起头，看了小满一眼，「九层以后再来看。」

小满四层，红木牌揭不得；白牌黄牌倒揭得，可轮不到他。他在两面墙底下站了半日，就看来来往往的人。天刚亮就有几个老师兄进来，眼睛只往白木牌上扫，手比眼快，一块好的白牌——「赤芝三朵」——揭下来便走，留给后来人的，是「黄芩一篮」这样跑断腿换一块灵石的。邓执事管这个叫「吃牌」，吃牌的人，叫老油子。也有人进来，白牌看也不看，只往红木牌上看，一个个脸上的皱纹比瞿老还深；一问，都是九层上卡了十年八年的，揭红牌，拿命换灵石，灵石换丹。黑线，多半画在红木牌底下。青木牌没人揭，一块「寻人」挂到起了霉，也没人摘。

正月里，家里的回信到了。坊市逢十九有集，蒙山来的信客在钱掌柜的铺子门口支一张小桌，收信，交信；他的家信，走的都是这张小桌。他娘的字小，写得密：屋顶修了；五两银子腊月里送到了，你爹便再没往黑松岭那头去过。末了一句是：吴婆婆让我捎一句话给你，她说：「告诉那孩子，牙还在。」我问她什么牙，她不说，只是笑。
story_full.en:
On New Year's Eve the abbey was half empty: those who lived near had all taken leave to go home for the New Year. That night he turned fourteen.

Zhou Heng broke his rule that night. In the stewards' office he lit a whole candle, not half, a whole one, called in the few disciples who'd stayed on the mountain, and gave each of them a bowl of dumplings. Cabbage filling, twelve dumplings to a bowl, no more, no fewer. Zhou Heng sat behind the table and watched them eat, and didn't touch one himself.

When everyone had finished they thanked him one by one and left. But Zhou Heng stood up, tucked the ledger under his arm and said, "Shen Xiaoman, wash the bowls." With that he went out towards the main hall.

Xiaoman washed the seven bowls, and only then noticed a ledger left on the corner of the table. Very old, a size smaller than the one Zhou Heng usually carried, its cover rubbed shiny. Zhou Heng recorded even how many pieces a candle was broken into, and had never left anything behind; and tonight of all nights he'd left this, lying open.

The page it was open at had gone completely yellow, and it was all small odds and ends: "beans, two sheng, fourteen coppers", "salt, half a jin", "Sister's hair string, three coppers". The writing was crooked and wobbly; one look told you it was a child's hand. At the end of the page there was only one line, but it was written so hard the strokes had gone through the paper:

**Eighteenth of the tenth month. The Zhang River. Sister.**

Xiaoman looked at it a good while before he worked out what was wrong. Every line in Zhou Heng's accounts was followed by a number: one herb, three spirit stones, half a candle. Only this line had nothing after it.

He shut the ledger, tucked it inside his robe and went to the main hall to give it back. The door of the hall stood ajar, and a lamp was lit inside. He had just reached the gallery when he heard Zhou Heng's voice. He had never heard that voice before: it didn't sound like keeping accounts, it sounded like begging. "...Abbot, this year, let me go."

The Abbot's voice was gentle. "It's ten days' road. What's in that river isn't something a Qi Condensation cultivator can deal with. If you go, the Zhou family will be one fewer again." After a while he went on: "That business in Ye: they call it finding a bride for the River Lord, but really someone is using the River Lord's name to squeeze money out of the common people every year, and behind the people squeezing stands a great sect. If one of the abbey's elders goes, that's the Sunken Cauldron Abbey falling out with them. If a disciple who came up from the outer sect takes a tablet and goes, that's only an errand. But whoever goes has to have Foundation Establishment, or he won't come back. In the outer sect, no one reached Foundation Establishment this year."

The hall was silent a long time. Zhou Heng said, "...Yes. Next year, I'll come again."

Xiaoman shrank back behind a pillar of the gallery. Zhou Heng came out of the hall, walking very slowly. Xiaoman held out the old ledger: "You left this." Zhou Heng took it, looked at him and said, "Did you read it?" Xiaoman said, "...Senior brother Zhou has good handwriting." Zhou Heng put the ledger inside his robe and walked away.

Xiaoman stood in the gallery a while. The eighteenth of the tenth month, the Zhang River, someone with Foundation Establishment: those three things he kept.

Later he heard about Zhou Heng from Steward Deng. Zhou Heng was from Ye. His father died early, and at home there was only him and an older sister. The year he was eight and his sister fifteen, the shamans of the River Lord's temple picked her, saying she was the bride the River Lord fancied. On the eighteenth of the tenth month, he chased that boat along the bank of the Zhang River for two li; the boat reached the middle of the river, tipped, and was gone. The next year he climbed Mount Meng with a bundle of firewood on his back, came into the Sunken Cauldron Abbey, and had stayed nearly twenty years. "It's not revenge he's after," said Steward Deng. "Every year that river still takes one more. He's kept accounts all his life, and that's the one entry he can't balance."

On the first day of the first month, spirit stones were handed out, and Zhou Heng sat behind the table at the dining-hall door giving them out. Xiaoman had gone into the inner sect's register, and by rights his outer-sect duty should be handed back, so he untied the night-watch token from his waist and set it on the table. Zhou Heng didn't even look at it, and pushed it back with one finger: "It'll only sit empty." After a pause he added, "Keep wearing it. If the garden's one plant short, the Discipline Hall asks you first."

Zhou Heng took another tablet out of the drawer and slapped it on the table. This one wasn't ebony but pine, a hand long, carved with three characters: Stewards' Hall. "Inner-sect people have one more thing on their account: errands. The errand tablets hang in the Stewards' Hall. Take one, do one job; when it's done, the tablet is turned over and you get paid the figure on it. Chores, the outer sect can take too; buying and escort, the inner sect takes." He paused. "The red tablets, for fighting demons: below the fifth layer, you may not take them."

The Stewards' Hall was west of the main hall, an empty room with no statues of the gods, only two walls.

The tablets on the east wall were ebony, all black, a hand long, the writing filled in with white chalk: "Kitchen · Helping", "Mountain Path · Carrying Water", "Scripture Library · Copying Sutras", "Pill House · Tending the Furnace", "Beast Pens · Feeding Spirit Beasts", "Talisman Room · Mending Talisman Paper". These tablets didn't involve fighting; they were outer-sect chores, anyone could take them. You took one and went to Zhou Heng in the stewards' office for the job, and the pay wasn't spirit stones but merit, a line in Zhou Heng's ledger; some were paid in goods, and kitchen help got a crock of pickles a month. On the east wall one nail was empty, and the white chalk under it was still there: "Herb Garden · Night Watch". Xiaoman stopped in front of that empty nail for a moment. Last autumn Zhou Heng had said in the stewards' office, "Herb garden night watch, Shen Xiaoman. Pay: spoiled plants, a basket a month," and he had taken it for a hard job Zhou Heng had handed out on a whim. So that tablet had come off this wall, and had been hanging at his waist all winter.

The west wall belonged to the inner sect, and the tablets came in colours. The white wood ones were buying: "Red lingzhi, three. Shopkeeper Qian at the market takes them. One spirit stone." The yellow wood ones were escort: "A cart of Xiapi herb merchants, by the north road. Three spirit stones." The red wood ones were demon-killing: "Spirit Herb Valley, north of Mount Meng: a demon at night, sixth layer, no spirit wisdom yet, eats spirit herbs, hurts people. Twenty spirit stones each." "North road out of Xiapi: the mountain road eats people, three lives. Three spirit stones." The blue wood ones were finding people: "West village, Pei County: boy missing, seven years old, a mole on the left ear. Five qian of silver." There were a few ebony ones too, about abbey business: "Scripture Library, airing the books, three days. Merit recorded." One against the next, like a wall of teeth. Some were turned over, with a vermilion "Done" on the back and a small board nailed below with a few names. Under some of the names a black line was drawn.

On the topmost row of the wall hung a single black tablet, with no writing, only a place name carved on it: "The Si River · The Ferry". Xiaoman looked at it a long time and couldn't make sense of it.

The steward who kept the Stewards' Hall had one arm, was named Deng, and sat on the threshold weaving straw sandals without looking up: "Understand it?" Xiaoman said, "The black lines are..." Steward Deng said, "The tablet was taken and the man didn't come back." He turned the sandal over. "Thirty years of the inner sect: eleven lines." Xiaoman asked again, "The one at the very top—" Steward Deng said, "That's a black tablet. One a year goes up, two at most. It doesn't say what the job is. The job, I tell you face to face." He looked up and gave Xiaoman a look. "Come and look again after the ninth layer."

Xiaoman was at the fourth layer and couldn't take a red tablet. The white and yellow ones he could, but they never came to him. He stood under the two walls half a day, just watching people come and go. At first light a few old senior brothers came in, their eyes sweeping only over the white tablets, their hands faster than their eyes. A good white one, "Red lingzhi, three," came off and away, and what was left for those who came later was "Skullcap root, one basket", the kind where you ran your legs off for one spirit stone. Steward Deng called this "eating the tablets", and the ones who ate them he called old hands. Some came in and didn't glance at the white ones, only at the red, every one of them with a face more lined than Elder Qu's. Ask, and they were all stuck at the ninth layer for ten years or eight: they took red tablets, traded their lives for spirit stones, and traded the stones for pills. The black lines were mostly drawn under red tablets. Nobody took the blue ones; a "Finding a person" tablet hung there till it grew mould, and nobody took it down.

In the first month, the answer from home arrived. The market held its fair on days ending in nine, and the letter carrier from Mount Meng set up a little table outside Shopkeeper Qian's shop, taking letters and handing them out; his letters from home all came by that little table. Mother's writing was small and close: the roof was mended; the five taels of silver had arrived in the twelfth month, and your Pa hasn't gone up towards Black Pine Ridge since. The last line said: Granny Wu asked me to pass something on to you. She said, "Tell the boy the tooth's still there." I asked her what tooth, and she wouldn't say, only laughed.

exits.means: feeds the spring culls (the 巡夜 pay, collected at the 执事堂 at the month's end) into the Rice Bucket: three qi pills of one, two and nine lines, the two-line to 孙二狗 and the nine to 阿禾; sorts the basket by herb and finds the three recipes (黄精+灵石 → 聚气丹, 黄芪+a breath → 回春丹, 紫玉参+a breath → 回气丹) — the recipe decides the pill, the grade is luck (mostly one or two lines, 2026-10-07); the jar fills on pills, 五层 is crossed on the cliff in the third month (定风), 灵石 run out before 黄精

story.zh:
好容易熬到开了春，药园开了园。周衡把一篮残株推了过来。他差不多全拿去喂了饭桶。半个月喂下去半篮，开出三颗[聚气丹]{注=qi-pill}，青白透亮。三颗一个样子，纹却不一样：一颗一道纹；一颗两道纹；还有一颗，他对着柴房门缝里的光数了三遍，足足九道。

他照师父的功课，每天天不亮上崖顶，站到巽那一格上，看落叶打转。到了三月里一个早上，一片叶子从崖边起来，往他脸上飘，他没躲，也没砍，只往旁边挪了半步。那天早上，丹田里那口缸「咚」地一沉，他过了五层。瞿老道：「定风。」

只有一样不省事：黄精月月有，灵石月月见底。他站在执事堂西墙底下，看那些写着「灵石」的牌子，头一回觉得那不是牌子，是丹。

过了两日，讲堂上阿禾和孙二狗的书案底下，各多了一个油纸包，包里一颗聚气丹。孙二狗那一颗，两道纹；阿禾那一颗，他没说——是那颗九道的。数到第九道，她的嘴唇停住了。她什么也没问，原样包好，揣进怀里，没有吃。

孙二狗却当夜就吃了。天亮的时候，孙二狗从练气零层，冲到了一层。他站在大通铺门口，瞧着掌心里那一缕细细的黄气，瞧得眼泪鼻涕一齐流了下来。两道纹的丹，是往那点潮上浇了一瓢水。瓢是小满的，井是他自己一夜一夜挖的。

这一哭，哭坏了事。一个零层的杂灵根，一夜引了气，不到晌午便传遍了外门，天黑前传进了内门。
story.en:
At long last spring came and the herb garden opened. Zhou Heng pushed a basket of spoiled plants across. He fed nearly all of it to the Rice Bucket. In half a month he fed it half a basket and got three [Qi-Gathering Pills]{注=qi-pill}, blue-white and clear. The three looked alike, but their lines differed: one had one line; one had two lines; and the last one, which he counted three times against the light through the crack of the woodshed door, had a full nine.

He did his master's homework: every day before dawn he went up to the clifftop and stood in the Xun square, watching the fallen leaves spin. Then one morning in the third month a leaf rose from the cliff edge and drifted at his face, and he didn't dodge and didn't cut. He just moved half a step to the side. That morning the vat in his dantian sank with a *thump*, and he was through to the fifth layer. Elder Qu said, "Settling the wind."

There was only one trouble: solomon's seal came every month, and every month the spirit stones ran out. He stood under the west wall of the Stewards' Hall, looking at the tablets with "spirit stones" written on them, and for the first time they didn't look like tablets. They looked like pills.

Two days later, under the desks of Ahe and Sun Ergou in the lecture hall, there was an oilpaper packet each, with a Qi-Gathering Pill inside. Sun Ergou's was two lines; Ahe's, he didn't say what for. It was the nine-line one. At the ninth line her lips stopped. She asked nothing, wrapped it up as it was, tucked it inside her robe, and didn't eat it.

Sun Ergou ate his that same night. By daybreak Sun Ergou had broken from layer zero of Qi Condensation to the first layer. He stood in the doorway of the common bunk, looking at the thin thread of yellow qi in his palm, looking till tears and snot ran down together. The two-line pill was a ladle of water poured on that damp. The ladle was Xiaoman's; the well he had dug himself, night after night.

That crying did the damage. A layer-zero mixed spirit root drawing in qi in one night: by noon it had gone round the whole outer sect, and before dark it had reached the inner sect.

story_full.zh:
好容易熬到开了春，药园开了园。月底他拿巡夜簿去执事堂交了差——东墙的差事，月底都是周衡坐在东墙底下收簿子、发工钱——周衡翻了翻簿子，在账上记了一笔，把一篮残株推了过来，巡夜牌上写着的工钱：黄精的烂根，黄芪的虫叶，当归的歪苗，篮底还压着两根紫玉参的断须。他差不多全拿去喂了饭桶，开出来的大半是灰和烟，没一点用处；他也不心疼，只当是摸它的脾气，喂一株，记一株，记着记着，觉得自己慢慢摸着一点饭桶的门道了。半个月喂下去半篮，开出三颗[聚气丹]{注=qi-pill}，青白透亮。三颗一个样子，纹却不一样：一颗一道纹，跟外门份例里每月那一颗一般；一颗两道纹；还有一颗，他对着柴房门缝里的光数了三遍，足足九道。

他爹说，打猎靠的不是运气，是脚印。他把剩下的半篮按样分成四堆，蹲着把这半个月的脚印一个一个往回认，认了一夜，认出三张方子：黄精搭一块灵石，出聚气丹；黄芪搭一口自己的灵力，出回春丹；紫玉参的断须搭一口灵力，出回气丹，丹田空了吞一颗，一口灵力灌回来大半缸。乱搭的，仍旧是灰。方子管的是出什么丹，不管出几道纹：同一根黄精，同一块灵石，这一回一道，下一回两道，隔上好几个月，才蹦出一颗三道四道的。九道的，开春那一颗之后，他再没见过第二颗。方子他一个字也没往纸上写，记在肚里。

打这以后，饭桶吐一颗聚气丹，他便吃一颗；一道纹的，丹田里那口缸涨一指，两道纹的，涨一指半。可缸涨了，层不动。他照师父的功课，每天天不亮上崖顶，站到巽那一格上，看落叶打转。头一个月，叶子转，他的眼睛跟着转；第二个月，他的眼睛不转了，叶子还转；到了三月里一个早上，一片叶子从崖边起来，往他脸上飘，他没躲，也没砍，只往旁边挪了半步——那片叶子贴着他的耳朵飘过去了。他看见了它起来的那一下。那天早上，丹田里那口缸「咚」地一沉，他过了五层。下一回上崖顶，他把这一下说给师父听，瞿老道：「定风。」缸是饭桶替他涨的，层是他自己过的——靠这饭桶的丹药，沈小满进步神速。只有一样不省事：黄精月月有，灵石月月见底——份例十块，饭桶又不是回回都开得出丹，十块喂进去，落到手里的没有几颗。他站在执事堂西墙底下，看那些写着「灵石」的牌子，头一回觉得那不是牌子，是丹。

过了两日，讲堂上阿禾和孙二狗的书案底下，各多了一个油纸包，包里一颗聚气丹。小满只说是利息：孙二狗那一颗，是牛棚里那半张饼的，两道纹；阿禾那一颗，他没说——是那颗九道的。

阿禾把那颗丹对着窗户的光转了一圈，嘴唇一动一动的，是在数纹。数到第九道，她的嘴唇停住了。她什么也没问，原样包好，揣进怀里，没有吃。

孙二狗却当夜就吃了。天亮的时候，孙二狗从练气零层，冲到了一层。他站在大通铺门口，把一只手摊在太阳底下，瞧着掌心里那一缕细细的黄气，瞧得眼泪鼻涕一齐流了下来。褚先生说过，他引气，五年起步；他进山门才半年。说书的替他算一笔账：这半年，他夜夜蹲在柴堆上数气，那口枯井底下，早磨出了一点潮；两道纹的丹，是往那点潮上浇了一瓢水。瓢是小满的，井是他自己一夜一夜挖的。

这一哭，哭坏了事。一个零层的杂灵根，一夜引了气，不到晌午便传遍了外门，天黑前传进了内门。
story_full.en:
At long last spring came and the herb garden opened. At the end of the month he took the night-watch book to the Stewards' Hall to report the job done (the east wall's errands were all collected at month's end by Zhou Heng, sitting under the east wall taking in the books and paying out wages). Zhou Heng leafed through the book, wrote a line in his ledger, and pushed a basket of spoiled plants across: the wage written on the night-watch tablet. Rotten roots of solomon's seal, insect-eaten milkvetch leaves, crooked angelica seedlings, and at the bottom of the basket two broken whiskers of purple jade ginseng. He fed nearly all of it to the Rice Bucket, and most of what came out was ash and smoke, no use at all. He didn't mind; he took it as getting to know its temper. One plant fed, one plant noted, and as the notes piled up he felt he was slowly getting the hang of the Rice Bucket. In half a month he fed it half a basket and got three [Qi-Gathering Pills]{注=qi-pill}, blue-white and clear. The three looked alike, but their lines differed: one had one line, like the one a month in the outer-sect allowance; one had two lines; and the last one, which he counted three times against the light through the crack of the woodshed door, had a full nine.

Father said hunting wasn't luck, it was footprints. He sorted the half basket that was left into four heaps by kind, and squatting there he traced back half a month of footprints one by one. It took him all night, and he worked out three recipes: solomon's seal with one spirit stone gave a Qi-Gathering Pill; milkvetch with a breath of his own spiritual power gave a Spring-Return Pill; a broken whisker of purple jade ginseng with a breath of spiritual power gave a Qi-Return Pill, which, swallowed when your dantian was empty, poured most of a vat of spiritual power back in. Mixed any other way, it was still ash. A recipe decided which pill came out, not how many lines it had: the same root of solomon's seal, the same spirit stone, would give one line this time and two the next, and only every few months would a three or four jump out. A nine, after that one in spring, he never saw again. He didn't write a single word of the recipes on paper. He kept them in his belly.

From then on, every Qi-Gathering Pill the Rice Bucket spat out, he ate. A one-line pill raised the vat in his dantian a finger; a two-line one, a finger and a half. But the vat rose and the layer didn't move. He did his master's homework: every day before dawn he went up to the clifftop and stood in the Xun square, watching the fallen leaves spin. The first month, the leaves spun and his eyes spun with them. The second month, his eyes stopped spinning and the leaves still spun. Then one morning in the third month a leaf rose from the cliff edge and drifted at his face, and he didn't dodge and didn't cut. He just moved half a step to the side, and the leaf floated past his ear. He had seen the moment it rose. That morning the vat in his dantian sank with a *thump*, and he was through to the fifth layer. Next time he went up the clifftop he told his master about that moment, and Elder Qu said, "Settling the wind." The Rice Bucket had filled the vat for him; the layer he had passed himself. On the Rice Bucket's pills, Shen Xiaoman came on by leaps and bounds. There was only one trouble: solomon's seal came every month, and every month the spirit stones ran out. The allowance was ten, and the Rice Bucket didn't produce a pill every time; ten went in and only a few came back. He stood under the west wall of the Stewards' Hall, looking at the tablets with "spirit stones" written on them, and for the first time they didn't look like tablets. They looked like pills.

Two days later, under the desks of Ahe and Sun Ergou in the lecture hall, there was an oilpaper packet each, with a Qi-Gathering Pill inside. Xiaoman said only that it was interest. Sun Ergou's was for the half flatbread in the cowshed, two lines; Ahe's, he didn't say what for. It was the nine-line one.

Ahe turned the pill once against the light from the window, her lips moving: she was counting lines. At the ninth line her lips stopped. She asked nothing, wrapped it up as it was, tucked it inside her robe, and didn't eat it.

Sun Ergou ate his that same night. By daybreak Sun Ergou had broken from layer zero of Qi Condensation to the first layer. He stood in the doorway of the common bunk with one hand spread in the sunlight, looking at the thin thread of yellow qi in his palm, looking till tears and snot ran down together. Master Chu had said that drawing in qi would take him five years at the least, and he had been through the gate only half a year. The storyteller will do the sum for him: for half a year he had squatted on the woodpile every night counting breaths, and at the bottom of that dry well a little damp had already been worn into being. The two-line pill was a ladle of water poured on that damp. The ladle was Xiaoman's; the well he had dug himself, night after night.

That crying did the damage. A layer-zero mixed spirit root drawing in qi in one night: by noon it had gone round the whole outer sect, and before dark it had reached the inner sect.
